attrs.title: Digits count bundles, positions name the bundle size

c:
Think of a shop that only uses bundles of three: loose items, packets of 3, boxes of 3 packets
(9 items), crates of 3 boxes (27 items). To record 46 items you fill crates first: one crate

of ten.

c:
Binary is the language of the hardware, but long strings of bits are hard for people to read.
Octal and hexadecimal fix that, and they fix it

you convert by cutting the bit string into groups, with no division at all. In this lesson you

between octal, hex and base 4 through binary, how to read a "powers of 16" sum straight off as
hex, and how to add, subtract and multiply directly in base 8 or 16.

chapters is written in these bases: memory addresses and instruction fields in hex, Unix
permissions in octal, K-map cells and register contents in binary. The 2's-complement patterns
of

is a dictionary: it says which bit string stands for which symbol. Plain binary is one
such dictionary, and a very good one for arithmetic, but it is not the best for everything.
In this lesson you meet the codes digital systems actually use for decimal digits (BCD,
excess-3, 2421), for positions and counters (Gray code), and for catching and fixing errors
(parity and Hamming codes). You will learn how to convert into and out of each, how to tell
whether a code is weighted or self-complementing, why a Gray code never glitches, and how three
parity bits can locate any single flipped bit in a 7-bit word.

arithmetic-shift.title: Arithmetic and logical shifts
arithmetic-shift.intro: The 8-bit pattern of −7, 11111001. Shifted copies will appear underneath.

steps.caption: Arithmetic shift right: every bit moves one place right, the last bit falls off, and the sign bit is copied into the empty top place. 11111001 → 11111100 = −4.
−7 ÷ 2 = −3.5, and the shift gave −4: an arithmetic right shift divides by 2 and rounds down (towards −∞), not towards zero.
A logical shift right fills the top with 0 instead. 01111100 = 124: fine for unsigned numbers, wrong for negative ones.
Shift left (arithmetic and logical are the same): a 0 enters at the right. 11110010 = −14 = 2 × (−7). It is exact because the top two bits of x were equal, so no significant bit was lost.

base-carry-column.title: Column addition in base 8
base-carry-column.intro: Two octal numbers lined up by place: 37 above 45. Carries will appear above the columns.

elements.text: Adding (37)₈ + (45)₈: a column that reaches 8 carries

steps.caption: Units column: 7 + 5 = 12. In base 8, twelve is one eight and four units, so write 4 and carry 1 into the eights column.
Eights column: 3 + 4 + the carry 1 = 8. That is exactly one 64 and no eights, so write 0 and carry 1 again.
Nothing is left to add except the carry, so it becomes the leading digit: (37)₈ + (45)₈ = (104)₈.
Check in decimal: 31 + 37 = 68, and (104)₈ = 64 + 4 = 68.

bcd-vs-binary.title: BCD versus binary
bcd-vs-binary.intro: Top: 59 in BCD, two 4-bit groups 0101 (5) and 1001 (9), each with weights 8 4 2 1. Bottom: 59 in pure binary, 111011, six bits with weights 32 to 1. BCD spends 8 bits where binary needs 6, and reading the BCD pattern as plain binary gives 89.

elements.text: 59 in BCD and in pure binary
read as binary, the BCD pattern 0101 1001 would be 89, not 59

code-tables.title: Decimal digits in four codes
code-tables.intro: A table of the digits 0 to 9 in 8421 BCD, excess-3, 2421 and 4-bit Gray code. For example 5 is 0101 in BCD, 1000 in excess-3, 1011 in 2421 and 0111 in Gray; 9 is 1001, 1100, 1111 and 1101.

doubling-peel.title: Repeated doubling: 0.625 to binary
doubling-peel.intro: We will double the fraction again and again. Each integer part that pops out is one bit after the point.

elements.text: 0.625 to binary: double, peel off the integer part

steps.caption: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.25 for the next round.
0.25 × 2 = 0.5. The integer part 0 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.5 for the next round.
0.5 × 2 = 1. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0 for the next round. The fraction left is 0, so the expansion stops: 0.625 has a finite binary form.
The bits come out first-to-last from the top, so read the column downward: 0.625 = (0.101)₂ = 1/2 + 1/8.

fixed-point-bits.title: Bit weights in a 5.3 fixed-point byte
fixed-point-bits.intro: Eight bit cells b7 to b0 with the binary point between b3 and b2. Weights above the point are 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; below it ½, ¼, ⅛. The pattern 01011.010 is 8 + 2 + 1 + ¼ = 11.25. The format covers 0 to 31.875 in steps of ⅛.

elements.text: Unsigned 5.3 fixed point: b₇ … b₃ . b₂ b₁ b₀
range 0 … 31.875 in steps of ⅛ (2⁸ = 256 values)

fixed-point-ruler.title: Fixed point: the range–resolution trade-off
fixed-point-ruler.intro: A number line from 0 to 16 with sixteen tick marks, one for each 4-bit pattern. Each step moves the binary point one place left.

elements.text: 4 bits, point moved: range shrinks, steps get finer

steps.caption: With 0 fraction bits (4.0 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 1 from 0 to 15: resolution 1, largest value 15 = 2⁴ − 1.
With 1 fraction bit (3.1 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.5 from 0 to 7.5: resolution 0.5, largest value 7.5 = 2³ − 0.5.
With 2 fraction bits (2.2 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.25 from 0 to 3.75: resolution 0.25, largest value 3.75 = 2² − 0.25.
With 3 fraction bits (1.3 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.125 from 0 to 1.875: resolution 0.125, largest value 1.875 = 2¹ − 0.125.
The count of values never changes: n bits always give 2ⁿ = 16 patterns. Moving the point only trades range for resolution.

gray-reflect.title: Reflected Gray code, built by mirroring
gray-reflect.intro: The 1-bit Gray code, 0 and 1. Longer codes will be built to its right, each from the one before.

steps.caption: Start with the 1-bit Gray code: 0, 1. The two codes differ in one bit.
Copy the list, then append its mirror image (1, 0) underneath. Put 0 in front of the top half and 1 in front of the bottom half: 00, 01, 11, 10.
Do it again: the 2-bit list, then its mirror, with prefixes 0 and 1. The result is the 3-bit reflected Gray code: 000 001 011 010 110 111 101 100.
Across the mirror line the two neighbours are the same code with only the new front bit changed (010 → 110). And the last code 100 differs from the first 000 in one bit too, so the list wraps round.

gray-wheel.title: Rotary encoder disc in Gray code
gray-wheel.intro: A disc cut into 8 sectors and 3 rings. Reading clockwise from the top, the sectors are coded 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100. At every boundary between neighbouring sectors only one ring changes between clear and shaded, so a sensor sitting on a boundary can misread at most one bit and is never more than one position wrong.

elements.text: inner ring = first bit, outer ring = last bit; shaded = 1

gray-xor-ladder.title: The XOR ladder between binary and Gray
gray-xor-ladder.intro: The binary number 1011 on top and an empty Gray row underneath.

elements.text: Binary → Gray: XOR each bit with its left neighbour

steps.caption: The first Gray bit is the first binary bit, copied: 1.
The second Gray bit (from the left) = first binary bit ⊕ second binary bit = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
The third Gray bit (from the left) = second binary bit ⊕ third binary bit = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
The fourth Gray bit (from the left) = third binary bit ⊕ fourth binary bit = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0. (⊕ gives 1 exactly when the two bits differ.)
So binary 1011 (eleven) has Gray code 1110. In one line: Gray = b ⊕ (b shifted right by 1).
Going back, each binary bit is the XOR of all Gray bits from the left down to it, a running XOR: Gray 101100 gives binary 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1 = 110111.

grouping-slider.title: Grouping bits into octal and hex digits
grouping-slider.intro: The seven bits 1011010. The red dot marks the radix point at the right end. Dashed cells on the left are padding zeros that will appear when a group runs short.

elements.text: Grouping the bits of (1011010)₂ from the right

steps.caption: Start at the radix point (here, just right of the last bit) and cut off three bits: 010. Three bits make one octal digit, and 010 is 2.
The next three bits to the left, 011, are the octal digit 3.
Only one bit, 1, is left. Pad it on the left with two zeros (that adds nothing to the value) to make 001 = 1.
Read the groups left to right: (1011010)₂ = (132)₈. Check: 64 + 24 + 2 = 90.
Now regroup in fours for hexadecimal, again starting at the point: 1010 is A.
The last three bits 101 need one padding zero: 0101 = 5. So (1011010)₂ = (5A)₁₆ = 5·16 + 10 = 90.

hamming-74-venn.title: Hamming (7,4) as three overlapping parity circles
hamming-74-venn.intro: Three overlapping circles named 1, 2 and 4. The seven regions hold bit positions 1 to 7: position 7 is in all three circles, 3 in circles 1 and 2, 5 in circles 1 and 4, 6 in circles 2 and 4, and 1, 2, 4 each in one circle only. The data bits 1, 0, 1, 1 sit in positions 3, 5, 6, 7.

steps.caption: Each parity bit makes its circle hold an even number of 1s. Circle 1 holds positions 3, 5, 7 = 1, 0, 1: two 1s already, so p1 = 0.
Circle 2 holds positions 3, 6, 7 = 1, 1, 1: three 1s, so p2 = 1 to make four.
Circle 4 holds positions 5, 6, 7 = 0, 1, 1: two 1s, so p4 = 0. The codeword (positions 1–7) is 0110011.
Noise flips position 6 (1 → 0). The received word is 0110001.
Recount each circle. Circle 1 is still even (it does not contain position 6). Circles 2 and 4 are now odd: they fail.
Add the numbers of the failing circles: 2 + 4 = 6. The only position inside circles 2 and 4 but outside circle 1 is 6, so flip it back. Syndrome 6, corrected word 0110011.

hex-nibble-table.title: The sixteen hex digits as 4-bit groups, with their count of 1s
hex-nibble-table.intro: Two tables. Left: hex digits 0 to 7, right: 8 to F. Each row gives the digit, its four bits, how many of those bits are 1, and its decimal value. For example 7 is 0111 with three 1s, and F is 1111 with four 1s.

horner-chain.title: Horner's chain: (257)₈ to decimal
horner-chain.intro: Start with a running total of 0. Each arrow will multiply the total by the base 8 and add one digit.

elements.text: Horner's chain for (257)₈: multiply by 8, add the next digit

steps.caption: Take the running total 0, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 2: 0 × 8 + 2 = 2.
Take the running total 2, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 5: 2 × 8 + 5 = 21.
Take the running total 21, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 7: 21 × 8 + 7 = 175.
Every digit has been used, so the last total is the value: (257)₈ = 175. The same total comes from 2·64 + 5·8 + 7, but without writing any powers.

msb-weight-bar.title: Place values of an 8-bit 2's-complement number
msb-weight-bar.intro: Eight bit cells with weights −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; the leftmost weight is negative. The pattern 10110100 has 1s under −128, 32, 16 and 4, so it is worth −76. The range is −128 to +127.

negate-invert-plus-one.title: Invert and add 1, and the copy-to-the-first-1 shortcut
negate-invert-plus-one.intro: The 8-bit pattern of +88: 01011000. We will build the pattern of −88 underneath.

elements.text: Negating +88 in 8 bits: invert, then add 1

steps.caption: Flip every bit of 01011000. The result 10100111 is x̄, and x + x̄ = 11111111 = 2⁸ − 1.
Add 1 to x̄. The three trailing 1s of x̄ turn into 0s as the carry ripples left, and the first 0 it meets becomes 1.
Compare x and −x: the rightmost 1 of x and everything to its right (1000) are copied unchanged; every bit to its left is flipped. That is the copy-to-the-first-1 shortcut.
Check: 10101000 read with the −128 weight is −128 + 32 + 8 = −88.

octal-hex-bridge.title: The binary bridge from octal to hex
octal-hex-bridge.intro: The octal numeral 546, one box per digit. Binary and hex rows will appear under it.

elements.text: Octal → binary → hexadecimal, never through decimal

steps.caption: Write each octal digit as exactly three bits: 5 → 101, 4 → 100, 6 → 110. Each digit is replaced on its own; nothing carries between digits.
Now forget the old boundaries. Cut the bit string into fours, starting from the right end (the radix point).
The leftmost group has only one bit, so pad it with three zeros on the left: 0001.
Read each four-bit group as one hex digit: 0001 → 1, 0110 → 6, 0110 → 6.

odometer-rollover.title: An odometer that rolls over at 3
odometer-rollover.intro: Four counter wheels, all at 0. Under each wheel is the place value it stands for: 27, 9, 3 and 1.

elements.text: A base-3 counter (each wheel shows 0, 1 or 2)

steps.caption: One count: the right wheel moves from 0 to 1.
Two counts: the right wheel shows 2, the largest digit base 3 allows.
Three counts: the right wheel cannot show 3, so it rolls back to 0 and pushes the next wheel on by one. The display reads 10, which in base 3 means one three and no ones.
Jump ahead to 26 counts: the three right-hand wheels all show their largest digit, 0222. That is 2·9 + 2·3 + 2 = 26 = 3³ − 1.
One more count rolls each of those three wheels over to 0 in turn, and the carry ripples into the fourth wheel: 1000 in base 3 is 3³ = 27. In any base, 1 followed by k zeros is b to the power k.

overflow-wheel.title: Overflow on the 2's-complement wheel
overflow-wheel.intro: The 4-bit wheel with 2's-complement values inside. The green band marks the non-negative patterns, the red band the negative ones; they meet at the seam between 0111 (+7) and 1000 (−8).

elements.text: Adding on the wheel: overflow is crossing the seam

steps.caption: Start at 0101 = +5. Adding a positive number means stepping clockwise.
Add +4: four steps clockwise pass 0111 (+7) and cross the seam into 1001. The pattern reads −7, but 5 + 4 = 9 does not fit in 4 bits. Overflow.
Start at 1010 = −6 and add −3: three steps anticlockwise cross the seam backwards to 0111 = +7. The true sum −9 is below −8. Overflow again.

Now 0101 (+5) + 1101 (−3). As unsigned steps that is 13 clockwise, which lands in the same place as 3 steps back (13 = 16 − 3): 0010 = +2. The band shows the short way round. The 13-step route only passes 0000 (a carry out of 4 bits, dropped); the seam is not crossed, so +2 is right.

Rule: a sum overflows exactly when it crosses the +7 / −8 seam. That can only happen when both operands have the same sign. (Chapter 5 turns this into a gate: carry into the sign bit ≠ carry out of it.)

place-value-strip.title: Place value: the same digits in base 3 and base 5
place-value-strip.intro: The digits 1 2 0 1 in four cells. Above each cell is its place value in base 3, a power of 3 that grows from right to left.

steps.caption: The first digit is 1 and sits in the 3³ = 27 place, so it adds 1 × 27 = 27. Running total: 27.
The second digit is 2 and sits in the 3² = 9 place, so it adds 2 × 9 = 18. Running total: 45.
The third digit is 0 and sits in the 3¹ = 3 place, so it adds 0 × 3 = 0. Running total: 45.
The fourth digit is 1 and sits in the 3⁰ = 1 place, so it adds 1 × 1 = 1. Running total: 46. So (1201)₃ = 46.
Now keep the same four digits but switch the base to 5. Only the place values change: 125, 25, 5 and 1.
Weighting each digit again: 125 + 50 + 0 + 1 = 176. Same digits, larger base, larger value: (1201)₅ = 176.

radix-solutions-grid.title: Counting radix solutions: every candidate pair, with the invalid ones explained
radix-solutions-grid.intro: Two tables of candidate pairs. A tick marks a pair that satisfies the equation and every digit limit. A cross names the rule the pair breaks: y = 1 is not a base, the digit 8 needs y ≥ 9, and the digit 4 needs x ≥ 5.

recurring-loop.title: Why 0.1 recurs in binary
recurring-loop.intro: The same doubling method as for 0.625, applied to 0.1. Watch the fraction that is kept after each row.

elements.text: 0.1 to binary never stops: the fraction comes back

steps.caption: The fraction left over is 0.2 again, the same as after the first row. From here the same four rows repeat for ever, so the bits 0011 repeat for ever.
So 0.1 = (0.0 0011 0011 0011 …)₂, a recurring binary fraction. Any finite number of bits only approximates it.

repeated-division-ladder.title: Repeated division: 2748 to hexadecimal
repeated-division-ladder.intro: We will divide by 16 again and again. Each remainder becomes one hex digit.

elements.text: Convert 2748 to base 16: divide by 16, keep the remainder

steps.caption: Divide 2748 by 16: quotient 171, remainder 12, which is written C in hex. This first remainder is the units digit.
Divide 171 by 16: quotient 10, remainder 11, which is written B in hex. Carry on with the quotient.
Divide 10 by 16: quotient 0, remainder 10, which is written A in hex. The quotient is now 0, so we stop.
The first remainder is the lowest digit and the last remainder is the leading digit, so read the column from the bottom up: A, B, C.

sign-extension-stretch.title: Sign extension keeps the value
sign-extension-stretch.intro: The 4-bit pattern 1101 at the right. Wider copies of it will appear underneath, lined up on the right.

elements.text: Sign extension: copy the sign bit into every new place

steps.caption: −3 in 4 bits is 1101: the sign bit (weight −8) is 1.
To widen to 8 bits, copy the sign bit 1 into the four new places: 1111 1101. The value is still −3 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = −3).
Widen again to 16 bits: twelve copies of the sign bit in front of 1101. Still −3.
Padding with zeros instead (0000 1101) would give +13: zero-padding is right only for unsigned and for non-negative numbers, e.g. +5 = 0101 → 0000 0101.

twos-complement-wheel.title: The 2's-complement wheel
twos-complement-wheel.intro: Sixteen 4-bit patterns arranged clockwise in counting order, 0000 at the top. The number inside the ring next to each pattern is its unsigned value, 0 to 15.

steps.caption: Each clockwise step adds 1. From 0000 to 0111 the patterns count 0 to 7, exactly as unsigned numbers.
Now step backwards from 0000: one step anticlockwise lands on 1111. A step back means −1, so it is natural to read 1111 as −1, not 15.
Reading every pattern with a leading 1 as (unsigned value − 16) gives 2's complement: 1111 = −1, 1110 = −2, …, 1000 = −8. The top bit now says the sign.
The only jump is the seam at the bottom: 0111 (+7) is followed by 1000 (−8). Crossing it is overflow. 4-bit 2's complement covers −8 … +7, sixteen different values, one zero.
Sign-magnitude reads the top bit as a sign and the other three as a size: 1000 is −0 and 1111 is −7. Two patterns mean zero, so only 15 values fit (−7 … +7).
1's complement negates by flipping every bit: 1111 is −0 and 1000 is −7. Again two zeros and the range −7 … +7.
Back to 2's complement: one zero, no gaps, and the wheel's clockwise steps are ordinary addition. That is why every modern machine uses it.
